entry.title: Combined summary - Convention for tagged hash tags in BIPs
entry.summary: In the realm of Bitcoin Improvement Proposals (BIPs), a recurring discussion has emerged regarding the convention used for tagging hashes within these proposals. Specifically, there is variability in whether BIPs utilize a numerical identifier or a descriptive name for their tagged hashes. Historically, protocols like BIP 458 have employed descriptive tags such as "HalfAgg/randomizer," which were in place even before the proposal was assigned a number. Conversely, more recent cryptographic BIPs, including BIPs 324, 340, 352, 374, and 445, have adopted the practice of incorporating the BIP number into their tags. This inconsistency raises questions about the best approach to adopt going forward. The debate centers on whether to continue using descriptive names or to uniformly apply numerical identifiers once a BIP is assigned a number. Arguments in favor of using the BIP number highlight its uniqueness within the ecosystem and its utility in making the origin of a hash evident in code or test vectors. However, opposition to this method points out that the specification may require alterations at the point of number assignment, necessitating additional adjustments across existing implementations. Additionally, it's suggested that tags might not need to be unique across all BIPs, potentially serving as a more general tool for domain separation within cryptographic applications. The dialogue also touches upon the historical context wherein BIP authors may choose different tagging methods based on whether an implementation exists prior to or concurrently with the writing of the BIP. This observation suggests a pattern where BIPs developed post-implementation retain their original tags, whereas those conceived without prior implementations tend to adopt numerical identifiers. Given this backdrop, there is a clear need to establish a standard or at least document community opinions to avoid repetitive debates with each new BIP. Such documentation would ideally delineate when and why certain tagging conventions should be adopted, contributing to a more streamlined and coherent approach across future BIP developments. The question remains open, inviting further input from the Bitcoin development community on how best to standardize or document these practices.
